title: Hongqi unveils 12C ultra-fast charging battery - electrive.com
content:
Hongqi says its new battery charged from 10 to 70 per cent in under four minutes during tests. The development marks another step in China's race to cut EV charging times with ultra-fast battery technology.
Image: FAW Hongqi
Hongqi has completed performance tests for a new generation of ultra-fast charging battery at 25 degrees Celsius together with Lishen Battery and FAW’s battery subsidiary, China Automotive New Energy Battery Technology. The companies aim to significantly reduce charging times to make electric vehicles more practical and address remaining barriers to wider adoption.
The new battery achieves a peak charging rate of 12C, allowing it to charge at up to twelve times its nominal capacity. To enable this, the developers combined a new anode with a specially formulated electrolyte to accelerate lithium-ion transport. They also applied additional measures, including a carbon-swelling coating and bulk doping, reducing the cell’s internal resistance by 15% compared to conventional cells based on the same chemistry.
A key challenge posed by extremely high charging currents is the resulting thermal stress, which Hongqi addresses with an intelligent, uniform liquid cooling system. This system maintains the temperature difference across the entire battery pack within a narrow range of no more than three degrees Celsius during charging. An adaptive temperature management system further adjusts flexibly to driving and parking conditions to maximise efficiency and minimise the energy required for cooling.
In performance tests, the prototype required only 3 minutes and 41 seconds to increase the state of charge (SoC) from 10% to 70%. For the range from 10% to 97%, the manufacturer states a charging time of just 8 minutes and 3 seconds. Upon market introduction, this system would outperform notable competitors such as
BYD’s new generation Blade Battery
, which takes approximately five minutes to charge from 10% to 70% and around nine minutes for a 10% to 97% charge.
The hardware is supported by a safety-focused adaptive charging control system that monitors cell temperature rise in real time and dynamically adjusts the power curve. Continuous closed-loop verification of voltage and capacity is designed to effectively prevent overcharging and overvoltage. The company describes the system as “a significant milestone in power battery technology innovation.”
However, the FAW Group has not yet disclosed when or in which production vehicles the technology will be deployed. This is already the brand’s second notable advancement in the battery sector within a short period, following the introduction of
a first prototype with solid-state batteries
just a few months ago. The ongoing innovation pressure underscores that reducing charging times has become a decisive differentiator for premium manufacturers in the competitive Chinese market.

title: Gravita consolidates recycling with Kathua plant closure – Batteries International
content: Gravita India is to close a lead recycling subsidiary in the north of the country on August 1 as part of a group consolidation plan. The company announced the closure of its Gravita Metal Kathua unit on July 27, saying the same line of business is already underway at the group’s Jaipur manufacturing facility. Kathua, in the northernmost part of India, provides integrated recycling facilities with battery dismantling, smelting and refining operations. The facility has a total installed capacity of 6,000 tonnes and produces high-quality lead ingots and lead alloys by recycling lead ore, lead concentrate, and lead battery scrap to meet specific requirements of original equipment manufacturers. Kathua has also benefited from financial incentives provided by the regional government of Jammu and Kashmir, which Gravita said enables the production of competitive products that exceed industry standards. However, Jaipur offers greater operational and cost efficiencies, Gravita said in documents filed with the National Stock Exchange of India. The decision is not expected to have any material impact on the group’s financial position. Batteries International reported in May 2026 that Gravita had posted adjusted consolidated EBITDA of Rs 452 crore ($47 million) for the fiscal year ended in March 2026 ― aided by a slight growth in lead sales. The lead recycler reported a 7% increase in sales in the lead segment of its business, amounting to 49,000 tonnes per annum in fiscal 2026. That came after Gravita announced the overall lead battery recycling capacity of its Mundra plant had increased to more than 145,000 tonnes per annum following an expansion project. title: Exide Technologies hails ‘ambition-to-action’ sustainability report – Batteries International
content: Lead and lithium battery producer Exide Technologies has hailed key milestones achieved in emissions reduction and recycling in its newly released sustainability report. The European battery major unveiled its ESG Report for 2026 on July 20 — just weeks after the company was re-awarded a gold award from global business sustainably rating provider, EcoVadis. In its latest report, Exide said it was “turning ambition into action”, highlighting improved carbon disclosure project (CDP) scores for both climate change and water security — advancing from ‘C’ (understanding of environmental impacts) to ‘B’ (measuring, disclosing and acting on issues to boost transparency, sustainability and risk management). The company also reported a 21% reduction in Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions compared with fiscal 2022 and said it remained committed to an interim target of reducing those emissions by 30% by the end of 2030. Meanwhile, there has been an increase in the share of recycled or recovered materials used in production from 74% to 77%, plus further investments in renewable energy projects. The company’s automotive division develops and manufactures advanced 12V battery solutions for internal combustion engines, hybrid vehicles and EVs. The portfolio includes advanced lead acid technologies such as EFB, AGM, and Gel, as well as lithium ion batteries supporting applications ranging from cars and commercial vehicles to motorcycles and boats. Exide has three advanced lead acid recycling facilities in Europe, with valuable raw materials remaining in continuous use, significantly reducing the demand for virgin resources, the firm said. All of Exide’s lead acid battery and recycling plants operate in compliance with legal limits for lead emissions into air and water. While not all facilities are currently subject to regulatory limits for sulfate emissions into water bodies, the company said it recognises the environmental significance of both lead and sulfate emissions. Energy consumption has increased over the reporting period, which Exide said has been driven by operational factors including a 2% increase in technical lead output and expanded recycling activities — particularly higher throughput in breaker operations. Further electrification of selected lead pots in certain plants also led to increased electricity consumption. However, Exide said it is closely tracking energy consumption as part of its ‘energy excellence program’ and looking to further increase the use of renewable energy. President and CEO Stefan Stübing said: “Over the past year, our focus has shifted from defining our sustainability framework to executing it in practice. “We have made tangible progress in integrating sustainability into our core business processes, including risk management, supply chain due diligence, and performance monitoring, supported by strengthened governance and data systems.” The post Exide Technologies hails ‘ambition-to-action’ sustainability report appeared first on Batteries International .

title: ITEN Solid-State Batteries Target Implantable Cardiac Devices
content:
Portable
Design & Manufacturing
French manufacturer's all-ceramic battery technology eliminates thermal runaway risk while delivering fast-charging capability for next-generation ventricular assist devices and neurostimulators.
July 28, 2026
4 Min Read
Illustration of ITEN solid-state battery implanted in human body.
At a Glance
ITEN targets 600 Wh/L energy density and 2+ Ah capacity for Class III implantable cardiac pumps and neurostimulators.
All-ceramic architecture eliminates thermal runaway risk and enables 80% charge recovery in under 20 minutes wirelessly.
UK's Ilika targets neuromodulation with 300 µAh batteries; ITEN pursues higher-capacity cells for cardiac assist devices.
France-based solid-state battery manufacturer
has launched a development program to adapt its technology for Class III implantable medical devices—think cardiac pumps and neurostimulators that operate inside the body for years at a time.
The move builds on ITEN's earlier work in medical applications. Earlier this year,
Battery Technology covered the company's breakthrough in powering smart contact lenses
, showing its expanding footprint across medical device categories.
Targeting the toughest requirements in battery design
Operating under the SOLIMED project within Europe's IPCEI Tech4Cure initiative, the development program tackles challenges unique to devices implanted in the human body. ITEN is engineering its solid-state technology to meet demanding requirements: safety, energy density, fast charging, reliability, and miniaturization.
The performance targets are ambitious: 600 Wh/L energy density, capacity exceeding 2 Ah, and 80% charge recovery in under 20 minutes. If achieved, these specs would represent a substantial leap for implantable device power systems, particularly for cardiac assist applications where ITEN plans to deploy solid-state batteries.
Related:
10 Ways Tech Can Help on the Campsite or Trail
Inside ITEN's solid-state battery manufacturing line in Dardilly, France. Credit: ITEN
All-ceramic design eliminates thermal runaway
ITEN's approach centers on a full-ceramic electrode architecture that differs fundamentally from conventional lithium-ion batteries. The company uses nanomaterials expertise to create stacked ceramic electrodes overmolded into battery modules, eliminating liquid electrolytes and organic materials entirely.
This all-solid-state design removes thermal runaway and flammability risks—crucial when a battery operates inside the human body for extended periods. The monolithic ceramic architecture also drastically reduces cell volume variation, which typically limits battery lifetime in conventional designs.
For cardiac assist devices, ITEN plans to develop battery packs with multiple modules and integrated battery management systems. The technology's intrinsic stability minimizes swelling and temperature increases during operation—addressing primary safety concerns for implantable applications.
Fast charging could mean fewer surgeries
Higher energy density could enable more compact battery packs suitable for internal placement. The fast-charging capability is designed to support transcutaneous (through-the-skin) wireless recharging, allowing implanted batteries to recover most capacity in minutes rather than hours.
Extended operating life is another key objective. Longer-lasting battery subsystems could reduce how often patients need surgical procedures to replace implanted battery packs—a meaningful quality-of-life improvement for people with cardiac assist devices, neurostimulators, hearing implants, and other active implants.
Related:
7 Portable Power Stations Worth Owning in 2026
"Implantable medical devices represent one of the most demanding applications for any energy storage technology," stated Vincent Cobée, CEO of ITEN. "This development program is a major milestone for ITEN and a strong validation of our core solid-state technology platform."
Rethinking packaging for biocompatibility
Beyond the cells themselves, ITEN's program will explore advanced battery packaging solutions. The company plans to evaluate new biocompatible overmolding materials for complete battery subsystems, potentially offering alternatives to the traditional titanium cases used for implantable batteries.
Combining solid-state cell technology, compact pack design, and biocompatible encapsulation could enable tighter integration in future implantable medical devices.
Illustration of SSB structure. Credit: ITEN
Competition emerging in solid-state medical batteries
ITEN is among the few companies worldwide with industrial-scale solid-state battery production capabilities. The company controls the entire value chain from materials and cell design to manufacturing, holding more than 40 patent families. But the company isn't alone in pursuing solid-state technology for implantable devices. UK-based
Ilika Technologies
has developed the
Stereax M300
, a miniature solid-state battery with 300 µAh capacity in an ultra-thin form factor (5.6 mm × 3.6 mm × 0.9 mm).
Related:
Advanced Battery Designs Shaping Wearable Device Evolution
Both companies use solid-state architecture for safety and reliability, but they're targeting different market segments. Ilika's Stereax platform focuses on low-to-medium power applications like gastric stimulation, vagus nerve stimulation, and neuromodulation devices. ITEN's program targets significantly higher capacity—exceeding 2 Ah—for power-intensive applications like cardiac assist pumps.
The capacity difference reflects distinct application demands. Neuromodulation devices typically need microwatt-to-milliwatt power levels, while cardiac pumps require substantially more energy storage to support continuous mechanical circulatory support. ITEN's 600 Wh/L energy density target and fast-charging capability (80% recovery in under 20 minutes) position its technology for these more demanding therapeutic applications.
Expanding into high-value medical segments
Cardiac assist applications provide the initial use case, but ITEN sees broader opportunities across the Class III medical device market. The company already develops and supplies batteries for Class I and Class II medical devices; this program extends its technology into the more demanding implantable device segment.
The stringent quality and reliability requirements of Class III devices could drive improvements across ITEN's entire medical device portfolio. The project also contributes to European technological sovereignty in healthcare innovation as part of the IPCEI Tech4Cure initiative.

title: Apexanalytix Benchmark Exposes Supplier Risk System Gaps
content:
Apexanalytix Benchmark Exposes Supplier Risk System Gaps
Prioritise Us
on Google
Four in 10 organisations only create compliance reports after an incident, audit, or executive request occurs (Image source: Getty Images/Sean Anthony Eddy
New data from apexanalytix shows 87% of teams lack automated risk scoring ahead of discussions at Supply Chain LIVE: The London Summit in September
It is simple: supplier risk can lead to costly operational disruptions. As new benchmark data from apexanalytix shows, procurement teams carry accountability for supplier risk without possessing the connected systems or validated master data to prevent incidents.
As a result, firms are stuck in a reactionary state dealing with supplier delays, financial instability and fraud instead of getting ahead and stopping these disruptions before they occur.
Key facts: apexanalytix benchmark data
87% lack intake scoring: Most enterprise teams rely on buyer judgment rather than automated, data-driven risk scoring during onboarding.
13% detect information changes: Only a small minority have automated tools to track supplier updates post-intake, leaving master data stale.
60% operate siloed systems: Risk alerts and vendor master data live in separate systems, with just 27% maintaining a unified supplier profile.
40% report reactively: Four in 10 organisations only create compliance reports after an incident, audit, or executive request occurs.
The findings come as procurement leaders prepare to address digital transformation challenges at
Supply Chain LIVE: The London Summit
in September 2026.
Broken processes lead to blind spots
Data from apexanalyix shines a spotlight on critical blind spots across the supplier life cycle, starting at the onboarding stage.
More than four-fifths (87%) of
enterprise procurement teams
surveyed said they lack access to data-driven, automated risk scoring at intake and instead rely on subjective buyer judgment.
When it takes weeks of manual effort just to pull a single supplier visibility report, they are forced to react to disruptions instead of preventing them.
Luis Grisales, Senior Vice President of Supplier Risk Solutions at apexanalytix
Another notable finding was that post-onboarding change detection is broken almost everywhere, with only 13% of leaders possessing
automated tools
to track updates, which means supplier information quickly becomes stale.
As a result, risk programs are left to rely on outdated records that fail to reflect real-world vulnerabilities.
“Procurement and Supplier Risk teams are often blamed when supplier delays or disruptions occur,” says Luis Grisales, Senior Vice President of Supplier Risk Solutions at apexanalytix.
“When it takes weeks of manual effort just to pull a single supplier visibility report, they are forced to react to disruptions instead of preventing them.”
“Most procurement organisations do not actually have a supplier risk program; they have a spreadsheet and a hope.”
Luis Grisales, Senior Vice President of Supplier Risk Solutions at apexanalytix (Image source: Luis Grisales via LinkedIn)
How to stop system fragmentation and reactive reporting
Operational blind spots are not helped by disconnected systems, with 60% of procurement teams stating that risk alerts and vendor master data are stored in separate applications.
Only around one in four (27%) organisations in fact maintain a unified supplier profile that connects risk alerts, ownership structure and supporting evidence in one central location, while 40% of leaders say that
compliance documentation
is generated only after an incident, audit or executive request occurs.
Bolting AI onto a broken data foundation doesn't fix anything, it just makes the guessing faster. The real shift is AI turned inward on the program itself: surfacing exactly where your own gaps are before an event forces you to find out the hard way.
Luis Grisales, Senior Vice President of Supplier Risk Solutions at apexanalytix
To address these operational vulnerabilities and help teams identify them ahead of time, benchmark data shows that organisations must shift toward an always-on control environment grounded in continuous data validation.
One way to stop manual triage is to establish dynamic
risk-scoring models
that automatically link external risk alerts, such as financial distress or compliance changes, directly to specific supplier records.
“Data goes in once, at onboarding, and then nobody is responsible for keeping it true after that,” adds Luis.
“Bolting AI onto a broken data foundation does not fix anything, it just makes the guessing faster.”
Recipients at last year's Procurement and Supply Chain Awards
Linking data resilience at Supply Chain LIVE
Overcoming fragmented data foundations and building resilient supplier networks will be just one of the topics taking centre stage at Supply Chain LIVE: The London Summit, hosted by Supply Chain Digital and BizClik.
The conference, which takes place on 8 and 9 September 2026 at the QEII Centre in Westminster, London, will gather more than 1,000 logistics, procurement and supply chain executives to explore digital transformation strategies.
Those interested in learning more should look for the panel session,
Supply Chain Management: What Strategy do You Need?
, happening on 8 September 2026 from 2:15pm to 3:00pm BST on the Supply Chain Stage.
Panel speakers will examine how organisations can unify risk management, eliminate manual triage and deploy predictive technologies to secure modern global operations.

title: Kia opens EV3 pre-orders in Mexico ahead of US launch
content:
Peter Johnson
| Jul 29 2026 - 8:45 am PT
Kia opened pre-orders for the highly anticipated
in Mexico, where the electric SUV will be built and shipped to the US later this year.
Kia EV3 pre-orders open in Mexico as US launch nears
On Wednesday morning, during President Claudia Sheinbaum’s “Mañanera del Pueblo,” or daily press conference, Kia Mexico’s managing director, Horacia Chavez, announced the Korean automaker will invest $649 million to produce electric vehicles in the region.
building the first prototypes
in March, Kia opened pre-orders for the EV3 this week, its compact electric SUV that will be produced in Mexico.
The 2027 Kia EV3 will be available in Standard Range EX and Extended Range SXL trims. The former uses a 58.3 kWh battery, providing a WLTP range of up to 436 km (270 miles), while the latter has a larger 81.4 kWh battery, delivering up to 605 km (375 miles).
Mercado Libre
, the Kia EV3 SXL is available to pre-order, starting at 767,700 pesos, or about $44,000.
2027 Kia EV3 (Source: Kia)
In the US, the 2027 Kia EV3 will be available in five trims later this year: Light, Wind, Land, GT-Line, and GT. The base Light version uses the same 58.3 kWh battery, which Kia estimates will provide up to 220 miles of range under EPA conditions.
Higher-priced trims, including the Wind, Land, GT-Line, and GT trims, will be available with the extended-range (81.4 kWh) battery with an estimated EPA range of up to 320 miles in the Front Wheel Drive models.
2027 Kia EV3 interior (Source: Kia)
All-wheel drive (AWD) will be optional on Wind and Land trims and standard on the GT-Line and GT variants.
Based on the 400V E-GMP platform, the EV3 Light with the 58.3 kWh battery can charge from 10% to 80% in about 29 minutes. The 81.4 kWh battery takes slightly longer at around 31 minutes. Kia’s electric SUV also has a native NACS charge port.
Kia will launch the 2027 EV3 in the US by the end of the year. We will learn prices soon, but the EV3 is expected to start at around $35,000, making it one of the most affordable EVs in the US.

title: Huffy’s kids’ e-bike makes a compelling case for pedal-assisted riding
content:
Micah Toll
| Jul 29 2026 - 7:45 am PT
For many parents, the idea of buying an electric bike for their kid might initially seem unnecessary. After all, didn’t we all grow up pedaling regular bikes without a motor?
But the more you look at today’s generation of young riders – and the role that e-bikes can play in getting them outside – the more compelling the argument becomes. Huffy is betting on exactly that with its Quantis Kids eBike, a 24-inch electric bicycle designed for riders aged 12 and up.
Priced at
, the Quantis isn’t trying to be a miniature electric dirt bike. Instead, it’s built around the familiar experience of riding a bicycle, just with a bit of electric assistance to make longer rides and steeper hills less intimidating.
The bike uses a lightweight aluminum hardtail frame paired with 24-inch by 3-inch knobby tires for extra stability and grip on everything from neighborhood streets to dirt paths. Power comes from a 250W rear hub motor fed by a 36V 7.8 Ah battery, providing pedal assistance or throttle power up to 15 mph. That’s notably slower than the typical 20 mph Class 2 e-bike limit, keeping performance well within beginner-friendly territory.
Other features include mechanical disc brakes, a Shimano six-speed drivetrain, a removable lockable battery, an LCD display showing speed, battery level and assist mode, and three levels of pedal assist.
Yes, it’s easy to say, “Kids should just pedal.” Many already do, and there’s certainly value in that. But one of the biggest barriers to riding is that cycling can simply feel hard, especially in hilly neighborhoods or on longer rides with friends.
A little electric assistance changes that equation. Hills become manageable instead of discouraging. Longer rides become realistic. Kids who might otherwise choose to stay indoors with a phone, tablet, or gaming console suddenly have a reason to spend an afternoon exploring the neighborhood or local bike trails instead.
Perhaps most importantly, they’re still able to pedal, which is something that should be encouraged.
Studies have consistently shown
that pedaling e-bikes continues to provide sufficient exercise. Plus, getting teens away from screens and helping them develop bike-handling skills also has the benefit of offering the independence that bicycles have provided generations of young riders. In this case, the motor simply lowers the barrier to getting out the door in the first place.
If that’s what it takes to swap an afternoon of screen time for an afternoon outside, it’s hard to argue that’s a bad trade.

title: Hyundai reveals IONIQ 3 prices start at $30,000, and it already looks like a hit
content:
Peter Johnson
| Jul 29 2026 - 6:50 am PT
Hyundai says the IONIQ 3 is attracting more customer interest than any vehicle it’s ever launched. With over 300 miles of range,
Hyundai’s
new high-tech infotainment system, and a starting price around $30,000, the electric hatch checks all the boxes.
Hyundai IONIQ 3 prices revealed in the UK
After the electric hatch made its first public debut “on the road” in the UK at the Goodwood Festival of Speed (FOS) earlier this month, Hyundai is starting to open orders across Europe and the UK.
The IONIQ 3 has received “the highest-ever level of customer interest recorded for a new Hyundai model,” the company said. That includes gas-powered and electric vehicles.
With orders set to open soon, Hyundai confirmed IONIQ 3 prices are expected to start at under £25,000 in the UK, or about $33,500.
Vertu Motors’ website
, the base Hyundai IONIQ 3 Standard Range model is already listed at £22,245 ($29,800).
It’s available in Standard or Extended Range versions with four different trim options: Advance, Premium, Ultimate, and N-Line Evo. The IONIQ 3 N, Hyundai’s electric hot hatch, will also join the lineup.
Hyundai IONIQ 3 (Source: Hyundai)
the Netherlands
, prices for the IONIQ 3 start at €27,995 ($32,000). It’s available with the same battery pack options (42 kWh or 61 kWh) and six trims: Select, Trend, Vision, N-Line, Prime, and N-Line Evo. Hyundai said the IONIQ will begin arriving in showrooms in late September.
As Hyundai’s first compact EV in its IONIQ series, the electric hatch is positioned as a smaller, more affordable sibling to the IONIQ 5.
Hyundai IONIQ 3 prices by trim and battery pack in the Netherlands (Source: Hyundai)
Although it’s part of the same lineup, the IONIQ 3 debuts a new “Aero Hatch” design that makes it distinct from Hyundai’s other electric vehicles.
The new look “reimagines the compact EV silhouette,” according to Hyundai. Not only that, but it also provides a drag coefficient of just 0.263, the best in its class.
Hyundai IONIQ 3 (Source: Hyundai)
At just 4,155 mm (163.5″) long, 1,800 mm (70.9″) wide, and 1,505 mm (59.3″) tall, with a wheelbase of 2,680 mm (105.5″), the IONIQ 3 is even slightly smaller than the new Chevy Bolt EV and Kia EV3.
Despite its compact size, the IONIQ 3 is more spacious than it looks, with a luggage capacity of 441 liters, which, according to Hyundai, is expected to “set the benchmark in the segment.”
Hyundai IONIQ 3 (Source: Hyundai)
Ashley Andrew, president of
Hyundai Motor UK
, said the IONIQ 3 will “open up electric driving to a whole new group of customers.”
“The fact that we’re already seeing record levels of interest before it’s even gone on sale tells us everything we need to know about its appeal,” Andrew added.
Hyundai IONIQ 3 interior with Pleos Connect infotainment system (Source: Hyundai)
Based on the same E-GMP platform as Hyundai’s other IONIQ models, the IONIQ 3 will be available with two battery packs: 42.2 kWh and 61 kWh. The standard range (42.2 kWh) provides a WLTP range of up to 213 miles (344 km), while the extended-range battery (61 kWh) delivers up to 308 miles (496 km).
Unlike the IONIQ 5, the electric hatch is based on a 400V architecture rather than an 800V one to cut costs.
Hyundai IONIQ 3 interior (Source: Hyundai)
With DC fast charging, the IONIQ 3 can still recharge from 10% to 80% in about 29 minutes with the standard (42.2 kWh) battery. The long-range (61 kWh) battery takes about a minute longer, at around 30 minutes.
The IONIQ 3 is also Hyundai’s first vehicle in Europe and the UK equipped with its new Pleos Connect OS and infotainment system.
Based on Android Automotive OS, the system is more like Tesla’s with a smartphone-like user interface.

The setup will be available with 12.9″ or 14.6″ center infotainment screens, plus an optional driver display. Like Volkswagen, Hyundai is bringing back physical buttons for climate control, audio, and more, located under the center infotainment and on the steering wheel.
Hyundai’s new system features an AI companion, Gleo AI, that learns and adapts to offer a more personalized experience.
Electrek’s Take
Starting at just £22,245 ($29,800), the IONIQ 3 is an affordable, practical everyday electric hatch. With Hyundai’s latest tech and software, it’s no wonder the IONIQ 3 is seeing record customer interest.
Will Hyundai bring it to the US? Don’t get your hopes up. The IONIQ 3 is designed and built in Europe for European buyers.
The Trump Administration’s import tariffs would make it too expensive, plus hatchbacks are a tough sell in the US with Americans favoring large trucks and SUVs.
While those in the US will miss out on the IONIQ 3, the IONIQ 5 is
America’s best-selling EV
outside of Tesla so far this year for a reason.
The 2026 Hyundai IONIQ 5 starts at $35,000, making it
one of the most affordable electric vehicles
in the US. Like the IONIQ 3 for Europe, Hyundai builds the IONIQ 5 locally in the US at its Metaplant outside of Savannah, GA, enabling it to offer it at lower prices.

title: Volvo drops lidar for good on EX90 and ES90, pays owner compensation
content:
Fred Lambert
| Jul 29 2026 - 6:50 am PT
Volvo has confirmed it’s dropping lidar for good on the EX90 and ES90, and it’s paying owners compensation for a feature they were promised but will never get.
In Norway, that payout is NOK 18,000 (about $1,900) per car, one of several market-by-market checks Volvo is writing after cutting ties with lidar supplier Luminar.
Owners get paid for a sensor that never worked
The EX90 and ES90 shipped with a roof-mounted Luminar Iris lidar unit baked into the hardware. The catch: the software features meant to use it never arrived, and now they never will.
Henrik Juel Teige, a spokesperson for Volvo Cars Norway, confirmed the decision this week. “Volvo Cars has ended its partnership with the company’s supplier of LiDAR technology and has discontinued its plans to develop LiDAR-based functions for the EX90 and ES90,” he said.
So Volvo is compensating the people who already bought the cars. The amount depends on where you live. Norway gets NOK 18,000 (~$1,900). Sweden saw a SEK 16,000 (~$1,600) price cut on affected pending orders back in November. In the US, owners are offered roughly $1,500 in optional packages, including SiriusXM and charging credits, a tire-and-wheel plan, or a maintenance package. Dutch buyers get €1,500 and Canadians get C$2,000.
It’s a quiet admission that customers paid for hardware that turned into dead weight on the roof.
Why Volvo walked away from Luminar
This has been building since last fall. We reported in November that
Volvo was set to ditch lidar for 2026 and that Luminar was furious about it
. Volvo terminated the contract entirely on November 14, citing supply chain risk and what it called Luminar’s failure to meet its contractual obligations.
Then the bottom fell out for the supplier. Luminar filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on December 15, 2025. Without a solvent supplier able to deliver and support the sensor, the lidar-based features Volvo had marketed were never coming.
Volvo insists the cars are still safe without it. “The company’s products can deliver a high level of safety and driver support, enabled by the cars’ powerful core computing coupled with their advanced sensor set, with or without a lidar,” the automaker said.
That sensor set is real. The EX90 still carries five radars, eight exterior cameras, two interior cameras, and 16 ultrasonic sensors. Losing the lidar removes one layer, not the whole safety stack.
Electrek’s Take
Predictably, a lot of people are reading this as a win for Elon Musk’s camera-only gospel. Musk himself jumped on it this week, responding to a fan’s post about the payout: “I did try to warn them. Humans drive using neural nets and optical sensors. Same is true for robot cars.”
But look at what Volvo actually kept. The EX90 and ES90 still run five radars each, plus a dozen cameras and 16 ultrasonic sensors. That’s not vision-only. That’s Tesla’s approach with a radar suite bolted on, which is closer to what Tesla itself keeps quietly
flirting with going back to
than to Musk’s pure-camera dream. Volvo didn’t validate the vision-only bet. It dropped one expensive sensor and leaned on the rest.
And Elon should be ashamed to respond to this:
Elon has the guts to comment on this as a win for Tesla?
First off, EX-ES90 still has several radars as part of its sensor suite.
Secondly, take notes, Elon. That's what companies do when they don't deliver on a promise. They compensate their customers.
You have been delaying…
Instead, he should take notes. What Volvo did, compensate owners for its failure to deliver features, is something he has been delaying to do for Tesla HW3 owners for years now.

title: China’s solar market heads for first annual contraction since 2019 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
The China Photovoltaic Industry Association says domestic installations are returning to more sustainable levels but expects both China’s market and global PV additions to shrink in 2026.
Vincent Shaw
29 Jul 2026
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Commercial & industrial
Highlights
Utility-scale
China’s photovoltaic industry entered a broad contraction during the first half of 2026, with production falling across every major manufacturing segment and domestic installations dropping sharply from last year’s exceptional level.
Speaking at the China Photovoltaic Industry Association’s (CPIA) mid-year review and outlook conference, former secretary-general, Wang Bohua, said the industry was undergoing a “deep adjustment,” but argued that the decline in installations represented a return to a more sustainable growth pattern rather than a reversal of the long-term trend.
China produced 538,000 tonnes of polysilicon in the first six months of the year, down 9.8% year on year. Wafer output fell 7.3% to 293 GW, cell production declined 21.9% to 260.7 GW and module output dropped 35.1% to 201.3 GW.
Prices also remained under pressure. By early July, polysilicon prices were 42.3% below January levels, while wafer and cell prices had fallen 28.7% and 27.7%, respectively. Module prices were around 3% higher, partly reflecting changes to China’s export tax rebate arrangements.
New solar installations reached 72.07 GW in the first half, down about 66% from 212.21 GW in the same period of 2025. The comparison was distorted by a rush to connect projects before China introduced market-based pricing for new renewable energy projects in June 2025.
Wang said the 2026 figure remained above the average recorded during the first halves of 2021 to 2024. Monthly installations were also more evenly distributed than in the previous five years, suggesting a shift away from policy-driven deployment surges.
The association maintained its forecast of 180 GW to 240 GW of new solar capacity in China for the full year, compared with around 315 GW in 2025. Even at the upper end, 2026 would mark China’s first annual installation decline since 2019.
Exports provided a partial counterweight to the domestic slowdown. China exported $17.18 billion of wafers, cells and modules in the first half, up 24.3% year on year. Cell exports rose 36.8%, while module export volumes declined 2.5%. Africa increased its share of Chinese module exports, reflecting a gradual diversification beyond established European markets.
CPIA expects global PV additions to decline 8% to 612 GW in 2026. China’s policy transition will account for much of the contraction, while grid congestion, curtailment and negative electricity prices are slowing project development in several international markets.
The association expects global growth to resume from 2027, with annual additions reaching 864 GW by 2030, equivalent to a compound annual growth rate of around 7% from 2026.
The transition remains difficult. Most manufacturers continue to face losses, grid constraints are limiting deployment, and new demand from emerging applications may not immediately absorb existing capacity. The industry’s recovery will therefore depend on both supply-side consolidation and the development of more flexible electricity markets.

title: US bans foreign-produced solar inverters - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
In the United States, the Federal Communications Commission Public Safety and Homeland Security Bureau has added foreign-produced power inverters to its Covered List, executing an immediate ban on equipment authorizations for unapproved foreign models over national security and hacking concerns.
Ryan Kennedy
29 Jul 2026
Markets & Policy
Technology & Products
Inverters
United States
Utility-scale
Image: Wikimedia Commons / CC SA 4.0 / Laura Veerde
The Federal Communications Commission Public Safety and Homeland Security Bureau
added foreign-produced power inverters to its Covered List
, triggering an immediate and absolute ban on new equipment sales in the United States.
This means any solar or battery storage project relying on an inverter made outside the United States that has not already received an official FCC ID cannot legally turn on or interconnect. Because there is no phase-in period, grandfather clause, or grace window, the regulatory pipeline is frozen today, forcing developers to halt active procurements and find new hardware vendors. Crucially, this applies strictly to new inverter model filings rather than an absolute freeze on all foreign-built components. Find a
fact sheet from FCC here
However, the restrictions apply strictly to prospective authorizations for new device models; existing inverter models already approved through the FCC process remain unaffected and eligible for continued import, sale, and installation. Because the vast majority of near-term utility and commercial projects rely on hardware models that hold pre-existing FCC equipment authorizations, most active builds will experience little immediate operational disruption.
The action effectively overrides the Department of Energy analysis from January 2026, which inspected 30 Chinese inverters and
found zero evidence of malicious hardware
. The White House interagency council determined that physical bugs do not matter because the risk is purely digital. The administration ruled that the wireless connectivity inherent in modern smart inverters allows foreign adversaries to push firmware updates that could shut down solar arrays remotely, making all foreign-assembled units an unacceptable threat to the critical power grid. However, the regulatory definition focuses specifically on networked equipment; hardwired or fully air-gapped field inverters that lack remote communication capabilities fall outside the scope of the Covered List determination.
The immediate practical result is a massive equipment shortage that will delay upcoming commercial and utility projects. Department of Energy data shows that domestic manufacturers supply only seven percent of the U.S. solar inverter market, leaving a 93% deficit that cannot be filled by local factories anytime soon. This impact will primarily materialize down the line as manufacturers introduce new product refreshes or next-generation hardware designs that require fresh FCC grants.
The hardware blockade hits right as developers plan to connect more than 58,000 MW of new solar and storage over the next year. Without certified inverters, fully built solar farms will sit dark and unable to feed electricity to the grid.
For asset managers and engineering contractors, switching to a domestic vendor triggers a dangerous regulatory loop with grid operators. Interconnection agreements are tied to the exact engineering specifications of a specific inverter model number. Swapping out a banned foreign inverter for a compliant domestic model constitutes a Material Modification under standard utility rules, which forces the project to the back of the line for a mandatory engineering re-study.
The ban targets where the physical hardware is bolted together, not who owns the brand name. The determination covers inverters produced in any foreign country, regardless of manufacturer nationality. The FCC is using the federal Buy American Standard definition of a domestic end product to enforce the restriction. This means an inverter from an American company manufactured in an overseas facility is completely banned. Conversely, a foreign-owned manufacturer executing final assembly inside a U.S. factory can still clear equipment authorization, provided the local manufacturing process satisfies the federal component value thresholds.
Messaging from the White House explicitly tied this action to the national race for artificial intelligence supremacy. According to America’s AI Action Plan, the massive scale of next-generation data centers is creating an unprecedented spike in power demand. Tech companies have been counting on rapid solar and battery storage rollouts to keep these data centers online without crashing local civilian grids. By cutting off the supply of core power electronics needed to connect these clean energy projects, this rule risks creating an immediate electricity shortage that threatens U.S. computing competitiveness.
The only way for a foreign-produced inverter to bypass this block is through an emergency Conditional Approval process managed by the Department of Defense or the Department of Homeland Security. Under this pathway, foreign-produced models may receive conditional authorization if DHS or the Department of War formally determines that the device or class of devices does not pose unacceptable risks. As
outlined in Annex A
, this pathway serves as an intentional regulatory bridge, granting conditional grants to foreign suppliers who commit to a binding, time-bound plan to shift assembly to U.S. manufacturing facilities.
To comply, manufacturers must open up their entire supply chain and firmware architecture to federal auditors to prove their code cannot be manipulated remotely before the FCC will unlock their equipment applications.
Further review of the FCC Covered List determination and accompanying interagency guidance clarifies that the restriction specifically targets networked power inverters with remote communications, data transmission, or firmware update capabilities. Equipment lacking remote control features—or utilizing air-gapped external control architecture—remains outside the security determination. Additionally, while the rule blocks new equipment authorizations going forward, Annex A
establishes an explicit Conditional Approval mechanism
managed through the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Department of Defense(DoD), offering foreign manufacturers a conditional waiver pathway if they undergo supply chain audits and submit a binding timeline to transition assembly to domestic U.S. facilities.

title: Serbia adds 61 MW of solar in H1 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
After the first six months of the year, Serbia’s solar capacity reached around 379 MW. While the country’s green energy market has been impacted by delays in permitting and grid connection processes, its prosumer market continues to grow.
Patrick Jowett
29 Jul 2026
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Highlights
Residential
Image: Sadko, Wikimedia Commons
Serbia commissioned around 61 MW of solar during the first half of 2026, according to data shared by the Association Renewable Energy Sources of Serbia (RES Serbia).
The country’s cumulative solar capacity stood at
318.3 MW
RES Serbia told
pv magazine
that as of the mid-year, prosumer solar capacity had risen to 147 MW, an increase of 21.1 MW on the start of the year, while there are now 223 solar power plants connected to the distribution grid covering 232.82 MW of capacity, an increase of 40.6 MW. These increases take cumulative capacity to around 379 MW.
Danijela Isailovic, RES Serbia general manager, explained
that Serbia’s green energy sector faced significant challenges during the first six months of the year, particularly in relation to permitting and grid connection processes.
In May, the Serbian government decided to
postpone new grid connection studies
for variable renewable energy projects until 2029-2030, which Isailovic said has proven to be a bottleneck for investors, delaying the realization of several projects and limiting the pace of new capacity additions.
Despite these challenges, Isailovic said the demand for new solar capacities remains strong, driven by households and businesses seeking to reduce energy costs and contribute to Serbia’s energy transition.
“The full implementation of the active consumers framework is a major success,” Isailovic told
pv magazine
. “It has already encouraged companies to take concrete steps toward integrating solar into their operations.”
Zrenjanin-based Linglong International Europe and Belgrade-headquartered HBIS Group Serbia Iron & Steel became the first companies to submit requests to Serbian transmission system operator Elektromreža Srbije to connect solar power plants to the transmission system under the active consumer status, Isailovic explained. Linglong has submitted a 39.9 MW request and HBIS a 63 MW project. To date, there are no solar plants connected to Serbia’s transmission system.
Isailovic added that there are other large-scale projects set to begin construction, including the 300 MW Brebex solar power plant and the 150 MW Solarina project, the latter of which was awarded under Serbia’s
second renewables auction
. Other projects in the pipeline include the
Noćaj 1 and Noćaj 2 solar projects
, from Fortis Energy and Construction, which will integrate battery storage.
There are currently 24 battery storage projects that have submitted complete requests for grid connection studies, with a total approved capacity of 4,530.6 MWh, Isailovic said, while several smaller projects are currently in the process of connection under Serbia’s existing Energy Law.
Looking ahead, Isailovic said she hopes certain regulatory challenges will be reduced in the second half of the year, allowing projects to move forward more smoothly.
“If these barriers are addressed, other green energy projects should be able to develop and be built according to plan,” she told
pv magazine
. “While the first half of the year has been marked by delays, the outlook remains cautiously optimistic, with expectations that Serbia’s solar sector will continue to grow.”

title: Fraunhofer ISE unveils propane heat pump concepts for multi-family buildings - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Fraunhofer researchers developed several standardized propane heat pump concepts for retrofitting multi-family buildings after finding that no single system configuration suits every building.
Lior Kahana
29 Jul 2026
Research & Development
Heat pumps
Example building with a central air-to-water heat pump | Image: Fraunhofer ISE
Researchers from Germany’s
Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems (ISE
) have developed a set of typical solution concepts for replacing gas and oil heating systems with propane (R290) heat pumps in multi-family houses.
The set of concepts form part of the LC R290 research project, in which Fraunhofer ISE worked with a consortium of 20 companies from the heating industry and housing sector to develop heating system replacements.
The research team examined example buildings from a portfolio of participating housing companies with heating loads ranging from 23 kW to 93 kW. Some buildings had individual gas apartment heating, while others had central heating systems.
They concluded that no universal solution exists and that system design must account for building size, available heat sources, space constraints, hot water demand acoustics, and safety.
“Due to the various challenges, such as the question of a suitable heat source or limited space, there is no single technological solution; rather, we have developed several solutions that can be applied,” explained Björn Nienborg, Project Coordinator at Fraunhofer ISE. “What’s important is a building-tailored system design including heat pump, storage, hydraulics, control, and heat distribution.”
As a result, the researcher developed several R290 heat pump demonstrators for different retrofit scenarios. For central systems, they designed an outdoor unit with 20% less propane refrigerant than comparable systems, increasing efficiency by 15%. Their indoor solution features a 28 kW brine-to-water heat pump optimized for a low refrigerant charge. For decentralized retrofits with a hydraulically connected heat source, they built a 4.9 kW apartment-level heat pump using a charge of 150 g of propane.
“The low charge of 150 g is an important value for minimizing the hazard potential when using the flammable refrigerant propane, thus enabling the use of heat pumps in kitchens or utility rooms – the typical installation locations,” explains Timo Methler, Team Leader for Building Heat Pumps at Fraunhofer ISE.
The solutions will now be integrated into a software tool for decision-making and design of heat pump systems in multi-family houses as part of a new project.

title: Why consumers are choosing solar over fossil fuels - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
People across the world have woken up to the fact that renewable energy is a source of local economic stability and energy security, particularly when it’s on their roofs, with a recent global survey finding two in three people now support renewable energy and storage investment.
Sonia Dunlop
29 Jul 2026
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
Residential
Utility-scale
Image: AGL
People across the world have woken up to the fact that renewable energy is a source of local economic stability and energy security, particularly when it’s on their roofs.
Two in three people now support renewable energy and storage investment. Even more tellingly, solar farms – occasionally a battleground for local opposition – are now consistently proving to be more popular in local areas than any other form of power generation.
This is according to recent data from the
2026 Ipsos Energy Transition Barometer
– a global survey conducted across 31 countries – and it provides a reality check that policymakers ignore at their peril.
As geopolitical turmoil again sends shockwaves through global oil and energy markets, driving up costs at the pump and on the grid, people worldwide are realising an inescapable truth: energy security is synonymous with economic security.
The headline figures are stark: three in four people globally are worried about rising energy costs, and half have been forced to cut back on other essentials just to keep the lights on.
This is a conversation about the immediate financial health of households and businesses. About their energy and petrol bills, this month, and next month. This is now.
For years, the energy debate has been framed through the lens of environmental necessity. That, clearly, is no longer the primary driver for the public.
If we accept that the public’s cries are for lower prices and greater energy independence, then we must accept that the status quo of volatile, expensive, imported energy that needs to be re-imported every few days is a failure.
The Ipsos data shows that the appetite for change is stronger than many decision makers assume.
A clear 60% of people now support energy independence.
People have realised that relying on volatile global markets, and the geopolitical tensions that come with them, is a recipe for economic fragility.
Anxiety regarding foreign energy dependency has spiked to 70%, driven by the immediate, concrete fear of conflict-induced energy price and supply shocks.
So, how do we deliver on the public’s demand for low prices and security? The answer, increasingly, is sitting on our roofs, in our back yards and across open spaces around our cities.
And that’s why the Global Solar Council has launched a new partnership with the Global Covenant of Mayors on Energy & Climate to turbo-charge residential rooftop solar and storage in 14,000 cities around the world.
For households and small businesses, the path to lower bills is increasingly rooftop solar and battery storage.
When we advocate for the mass deployment of solar and batteries, we are not just advocating for increased generation capacity, we are advocating for the democratisation of power. For Resilience. For self-sufficiency.
We are putting the ability to slash energy bills directly into the hands of the consumer, and in a way that means they will see the benefits next month.Building reliable energy systems rooted in domestic generation instead of rollercoaster commodity markets.
Through this lens, national roadmaps to transition away from old-fashioned energy are no longer optional green initiatives; they are the most effective economic policies available to us.
Whether it is efficient heat pump incentives – backed by 58% of the public – or the rollout of solar and storage, people are signalling that they want off the fossil fuel treadmill. They are tired of being hostages to global energy prices that they cannot control.
Support for renewable energy and electrification is deep and broad across many of the biggest countries in Europe, Asia and the Americas.
Governments and decision makers in these countries need to understand the depth to this shift in public opinion and acknowledging the energy transition is an economic imperative for energy security and affordability.
If we want to build a consensus that lasts, we need to start talking to people about their bills and what can be done to cut them. In countries that are democracies, and in those that aren’t.
With the economic toll of our current energy model becoming harder to ignore, the shift to clean energy is an acceleration already well underway.
The data shows us that the public is ready to embrace renewable energy, because they realise it is the smartest way to keep their lights on, their costs down, and their independence secure.
The technology is ready and the economics are compelling. It’s time for policy to catch up.
Note on the
Ipsos Energy Transition Barometer 2026 polling
The polling represents the results of a 31-country survey conducted by Ipsos of more than 46,000 adults across: Argentina, Australia, Belgium, Brazil, Canada, Chile, Colombia, France, Germany, Great Britain, Hungary, India, Indonesia, Ireland, Italy, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, Netherlands, New Zealand, Peru, Poland, Singapore, South Africa, South Korea, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Thailand, Türkiye, and the United States.
The views and opinions expressed in this article are the author’s own, and do not necessarily reflect those held by
pv magazine

title: Financing secured for Timor-Leste’s first solar-storage project - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
The Asian Development Bank, World Bank and investors from Canada and Japan have partnered on a $85.7 million financing package for Timor-Leste’s first independent power project.
Patrick Jowett
29 Jul 2026
Applications & Installations
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
Dili, capital of Timor-Leste | Image: Jaime Gusmao
An $85.7 million financing package has been signed off for a 73.7 MWac grid-connected solar plant tied to an 80.2 MWh battery energy storage system in Timor-Leste.
The project is both Timor-Leste’s first utility-scale solar-plus-storage project and its first independent power producer project. It will be operated by Manatuto Renewables Power, a joint venture company between French utility EDF and Japan’s Itochu Corporation.
The funding package will support the development, construction, operation and maintenance of the solar-plus-storage system and association transmission lines and ancillary facilities.
It consists of $12.2 million in senior loans from the Asian Development Bank (ADB), $19 million from the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and $12.2 million from the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA).
The agreement also includes concessional loans including a total of $21.2 million from ADB’s Leading Asia’s Private Infrastructure Fund 2, supported by JICA, and Canadian Climate and Nature Fund for the Private Sector in Asia (CANPA), supported by the Canadian government.
An additional $21.2 million comes from the World Bank Group’s International Development Association’s Private Sector Window and the IFC Concessional Capital Window.
Electricity generated by the project will be sold to state utility Eletricidade de Timor Leste Empresa Pública under a 25-year power purchase agreement. The electricity generated is expected to be equivalent to the typical consumption of approximately 80,000 households in the country.
As the country’s first large-scale hybrid renewable project, the site is also set to reduce the country’s reliance on imported diesel. As of 2024, fossil fuels made up almost all of Timor-Leste’s energy mix.
Timor-Leste had installed 1 MW of solar by the end of last year, according to figures published by the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), up from 0 MW at the end of the year prior.

title: Italy gives 599 MW agrivoltaic project positive environmental assessment - pv magazine Global

Italy’s Ministry of the Environment and Energy Security has given a positive environmental impact assessment to a planned 599 MW agrivoltaic plant in Puglia, subject to several conditions.

29 Jul 2026

Italy’s Ministry of the Environment and Energy Security (MASE) has granted a positive environmental impact assessment to a proposed 599 MW agrivoltaic plant.
The plant will be developed by Spanish company Solaria as part of its Spinazzola project in Puglia, southern Italy. The favourable opinion of the project was given via
Decree 478/2026
Solaria initially submitted an application to MASE in December 2024 for a 669.99 MW plant.
Following a review phase and opinions from both local authorities and Italy’s Ministry of Culture Superintendency, the plant’s capacity was gradually reduced first to 630.11 MW, then to 611 MW, and finally to its current 599 MW, meaning its planned capacity has been deducted by around 10% during the consultation phase.

However, following the issuing of
opinion 987/2026
Conditions to be met include the removal of lots and rows of panels to create ecological corridors, compensation of at least 30% of the field area, a no-build zone around the 21-Archi Bridge and a redesigned landscape design. Preventive archaeological excavation requirements also remain.

title: Bhutan tenders solar systems for three schools - pv magazine Global
content:

title: German battery manufacturer files for self-administered insolvency - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
German battery manufacturer Varta has filed for self-administered insolvency, with the proceedings covering its solar-storage and energy management business.
Ralph Diermann
29 Jul 2026
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
Image: Varta AG
German battery manufacturer Varta has filed for self-administered insolvency with the Stuttgart District Court in Germany after citing a structural financing gap.
The filing covers the parent company Varta AG and all subsidiaries except Varta Consumer Batteries, which manufactures household batteries and power banks.
Varta Storage, which bundles the company’s solar storage and energy management system business, is also included in the proceedings. The company manufactures its storage systems in Nördlingen, near Augsburg, Germany.
Varta attributed the filing to significantly deteriorating market conditions, weaker demand, adverse currency effects, and the decision by a key customer to end its business relationship. The customer is Apple, which sourced batteries from Varta for its headphones.
The company also said the group’s complex internal corporate structure has made restructuring more difficult. According to Varta, these factors together resulted in a structural financing gap at the parent company level.
Varta said it intends to continue operating its business without restriction within the framework of the insolvency proceedings. Production, service, deliveries, and customer and partner support are expected to continue under the applicable insolvency rules. The company also said wages and salaries will continue to be paid. Varta currently employs around 3,300 people.
Under Germany’s self-administered insolvency process, the company’s management remains in office while a court-appointed supervisor oversees the proceedings instead of an insolvency administrator. The Stuttgart District Court appointed Stuttgart-based lawyer Tobias Wahl as supervisor.

title: World's only floating nuclear plant passes key safety audit in Russia
content:
International inspectors have completed a safety review of the Akademik Lomonosov.
International inspectors have finished a two-week safety review of Russia’s floating nuclear power plant, the Akademik Lomonosov. A team of thirteen specialists from the Moscow Center of the World Association of Nuclear Operators conducted the evaluation in the Arctic port of Pevek.
At the same time, a representative from China inspected the facility’s administrative division in Saint Petersburg. The auditing body, established in 1989, works globally to promote safety standards across nuclear facilities. During the audit, experts observed daily operations and examined technical documentation across several core domains.
“The international team focused on such critical areas as the organization and administration, maintenance and repairs, engineering support, radiation protection, operating experience, emergency preparedness, and other fields,” said Rosatom in a
press release
The final report noted fewer technical areas needing improvement compared to the previous evaluation conducted in 2022.
On par with top nuclear plants
“These findings rank the FNPP on par with Russia’s top nuclear power plants, including the Balakovo and Kalinin NPPs,” added Viktor Yelagin, Director of the FNPP.
“They highlight the exceptional expertise of the plant’s management and team, who maintain safety and operational standards in line with both Russian and global best practices.”
Named after the 18th-century Russian scientist Mikhail Lomonosov, the vessel, which is also the world’s only operating
floating nuclear plant
, acts as a mobile generation node for isolated coastal communities in extreme polar environments. It supplies both electricity and district heating to the local grid. Instead of using conventional ground-based foundations, the facility combines naval vessel design with small modular reactor technology.

Reactor system with safety features
“A nuclear floating power unit (FPU) is equipped with two KLT-40S reactor systems (each with a 35 MWe capacity) similar to those used on icebreakers,” explained FNPP.
Each reactor delivers an electrical capacity of 35 megawatts, providing a combined capacity of 70 megawatts for the entire plant. Thermal energy from the steam systems is also diverted to supply heat to nearby municipal networks.
Reinforced containment barriers enclose the reactor cooling loops and steam generators, protecting the machinery against severe Arctic storms, wave motion, and mechanical shock.
The reactors use a three-year refueling interval, which allows for longer periods of continuous operation between fuel changes. The vessel has an intended service life of 40 years, with engineering options to extend operation to 50 years.
Dedicated internal storage compartments inside the hull safely hold

Sustainable long-term plan
The facility’s long-term plan prevents environmental accumulation in the far north. Once the plant reaches the end of its operational lifespan, tugboats will tow the entire barge to a specialized shipyard for decommissioning.
Technicians will remove all spent nuclear fuel and radioactive waste, transferring them to designated storage facilities on mainland Russia.

title: Scientists Reveal the Climate “Perfect Storm” Behind an Ancient Civilizational Collapse
content:
Drought in the marshes of present-day Southern Iraq. Credit: John Wreford/Mosthotos
Overlapping climate cycles may have intensified the droughts surrounding the Late Bronze Age collapse.
Around 3,200 years ago, societies across the Eastern Mediterranean faced drought severe enough to strain water supplies, agriculture, and food security.
Research from
Stockholm University
, published in
Science Advances
, suggests these extreme conditions developed not from one isolated event, but when several natural climate cycles aligned and intensified an already drying environment. The findings provide new context for the Late Bronze Age collapse and may help scientists assess drought threats in a warming world.
“Rather than being caused by a single climatic event, we found that the most extreme droughts emerged when natural climate cycles operating over different timescales coincided. This helps explain why the drought associated with the Late Bronze Age collapse was so severe,” says Katherine Power, PhD student, Department of Physical Geography, Stockholm University, and first author of the study.
Climate modeling reveals a long decline
About 3,200 years ago, widespread societal collapse affected several major Eastern Mediterranean civilizations, including the Mycenaeans, Minoans and Hittite Empire. Severe drought has long been associated with this upheaval, but the climate mechanisms that produced it have remained uncertain.
Katherine Power and study co-author Qiong Zhang, professor in paleoclimate modeling in Stockholm University’s Department of Physical Geography, investigated the question with a state-of-the-art climate model that reconstructed changes across the Mediterranean during the past 8,000 years.
“Our results show that the region underwent a gradual drying trend over thousands of years, driven by slow changes in Earth’s orbit. Superimposed on this long-term trend, we also found shorter-term fluctuations in the Atlantic Ocean and atmosphere,” says Katherine Power.
The Eastern Mediterranean dried as part of a broader climate transition; weakening monsoons and shifting atmospheric circulation reduced moisture from Africa and rainfall across the region. Credit: Katherine Power/Stockholm University
Overlapping cycles intensified extreme drought
The reconstruction indicated that the harshest droughts developed when several natural climate cycles temporarily came into alignment. Their combined effects reinforced one another, creating dry periods much more severe than the gradual long-term decline alone would have produced.
“The convergence of these processes pushed the Eastern Mediterranean beyond a critical hydroclimatic threshold, reducing water availability and increasing pressure on agriculture and food security within already vulnerable societies,” Katherine Power says.
Natural variability could amplify future risk
The results offer a different way to understand major droughts of the past, while also carrying implications for present climate risks.
“The Mediterranean is one of the world’s climate change hotspots and the area is projected to become warmer and drier during the coming century. Our findings suggest that future drought risk may depend not only on long-term human-driven warming, but also on how natural variability in the Atlantic Ocean interacts with that background trend,” Katherine Power explains.
Reference: “Holocene ocean-atmosphere coupling and Mediterranean sensitivity to Atlantic circulation: Lessons from the Late Bronze Age collapse” by Katherine Power and Qiong Zhang, 24 July 2026,
Science Advances
DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aed5439
This work was supported by the Swedish Research Council (Vetenskapsrådet, grant no. 2022-03129). The data analyses were performed using resources provided by the ECMWF’s computing and archive facilities and the National Academic Infrastructure for Supercomputing in Sweden (NAISS), partially funded by the Swedish Research Council through grant agreement no. 2022-06725.

title: Archaeology Students Discover Rare 400-Year-Old Intact Pot
content:
Students found a small, intact clay pot — likely of Indigenous origin — during a field course instructed by archaeologists at the Florida Museum of Natural History. Credit: Kristen Grace
A rare intact pot is helping archaeologists reconstruct life and cultural exchange at Mission San Francisco de Potano.
Four centuries after someone shaped a small clay vessel by hand,
University of Florida
students lifted it from the soil completely intact. The pot, likely made by a member of the Indigenous Potano-Timucua tribe, is compact enough to sit in one palm. Its maker formed a narrow crease around the plain rim and smoothed the gray surface without adding decoration. What the vessel once contained, who used it, and why it was left underground may never be known.
“It’s very unique. Typically, we find things that were broken and discarded,” said Gifford Waters, collections manager for historical archaeology at the Florida Museum of Natural History. “You don’t leave things behind that you can still use, so why was this purposefully put into a pit?”
Based on its depth and location, the pot was likely crafted while the mission was in operation, but its style is not one the archaeologists are familiar with. Credit: Gifford Waters
Waters has handled complete objects recovered from shipwrecks, where intact materials are more common, but this was the first time he had worked with an excavation crew that found an unbroken pottery vessel. Even pots discarded whole rarely survive on land. Centuries of soil pressure, farming, construction, and shifting earth usually crack or crush them before archaeologists arrive.
Students recover a rare intact pot
The discovery came during a field course taught by Waters and Charles Cobb, curator of historical archaeology at the museum. Each Friday throughout the spring semester, University of Florida students traveled to Mission San Francisco de Potano in northwest Gainesville to learn the essential techniques of archaeological excavation.
An archaeology field course offers students a hands-on learning opportunity through the excavation of a centuries-old Potano-Timucua village and Spanish mission site near Gainesville. Credit: Brooke Bowser
The former mission now lies beneath a shaded woodland. Small 1-by-1 meter excavation squares mark places where students carefully remove soil with trowels, while narrow paths wind between the remains of a 17th-century kitchen, a friar’s residence, and the surrounding Potano village.
A Potano village became a mission
The Potano, part of the Timucua people of North Florida, moved to the site in 1585 after Spanish forces displaced them from their homeland, probably located between present-day Payne’s Prairie and Orange Lake. In 1606, the Spanish government sent a friar to establish a mission in the village.
It became one of the earliest of more than 100
Catholic missions
founded during the following century to reinforce Spanish control of Florida. Mission San Francisco de Potano was abandoned in 1706 and gradually disappeared from view until
artifacts began resurfacing in the 1950s
In the same site as the small, intact pot, students also found broken pieces of a much larger vessel that was likely brought to the site by trade or migration. Credit: Kristen Grace
At its height, the village likely held several hundred Potano residents and only one European, the mission friar. That population balance is reflected in the archaeological record. Most of the more than 7,000 artifacts recovered since 2006 are fragments of Native American pottery. Other discoveries include glass beads, stone tools, nails, and animal bones from meals containing turtle, freshwater fish, turkey, and other foods.
“What tells us the most is not just the artifacts but the evidence of activities. Knowing that we have a bunch of pieces of bone at the site is great, but the fact we know that nearly all of them came from one spot tells us it was a cooking area and trash pit,” Waters said. “It’s not just artifacts themselves but where they were on the site, how they were distributed and what they were associated with that tells the story.”
Whether due to human activities or the pressure of being underground, most pottery artifacts end up broken before archaeologists have the chance to uncover them. Credit: Kristen Grace
Context narrows the pot’s story
Although the intact vessel offers few direct clues about its original purpose, the place where students found it connects the object to a larger history. It came from inside a Spanish-made structure whose function remains uncertain and will require further excavation to identify.
Historical records show that a small group of soldiers was stationed at the mission after British attacks intensified in the early 1700s. The structure may have served as a barracks, an interpretation supported by the rear sight of a gun and a musket side plate discovered nearby.
Light scorch marks on the exterior may have formed if the pot was placed near a fire to heat up food. Credit: Kristen Grace
Its depth and position indicate that the pot was probably made during the mission’s century-long existence. However, archaeologists do not recognize its style, and they have not determined how people used it.
Cooking vessels often retain layers of burned food or charcoal inside. This pot has no such residue, suggesting it was not placed directly over flames. It may still have played a role during meals. Faint scorch marks could have formed while the vessel was being fired and hardened, or when someone placed it beside a fire to warm an individual serving of food.
Residue from burnt foods can provide archaeologists with clues as to what pottery vessels were once used for. Credit: Kristen Grace
Pottery records movement and cultural change
Soon after recovering the small vessel, the students found fragments from a much larger pot with markedly different characteristics. Its rough exterior and unusual material do not match known local pottery traditions.
Archaeologists think the larger vessel may have reached the mission through trade with communities in St. Augustine or present-day Jacksonville. Another possibility is that a newcomer carried it to the village while bringing different pottery traditions. The contrasting objects reflect how people, materials, and ideas moved through the settlement and became preserved in the soil.
“During the later years of this mission, folks from different parts of Florida and Native Americans from different areas moved into and around the site. It’s really neat to see these differences and connections in the artifacts,” Waters said. “It shows both the persistence and change of traditions over time.”
